name: The vocative comma: 'Let's eat, Grandma!'
scope: The canonical direct-address comma, the load-bearing exemplar of the whole bank. T1: the quoted contrast -- 'Let's eat, Grandma!' vs 'Let's eat Grandma!' -- and the answer names the missing comma of direct address (a vocative comma) with an in-stem example so the term is TAUGHT not assumed. T2: the same rule with a different quoted line -- 'I love cooking my family and my pets.' -- fix by inserting commas around 'my family' so the family is spoken TO, not cooked. T2b: 'Attention students, class is cancelled' -- missing comma of address (should be 'Attention, students, class is cancelled') vs the (wrong) reading that 'Attention students' is a class of students. T3: sentence-INTERIOR vocative -- 'I already told you, Marcus, to feed the dog' vs 'I already told you Marcus to feed the dog' (in the wrong version, the speaker is telling someone else to feed a dog named Marcus). T3b: quoted-speech tag vocative -- 'Please, Dad, can I go?' where the commas around 'Dad' are what mark it as address, not narration. T4: distinguish vocative comma from appositive comma with a stem that quotes 'Come here, my brother!' -- vocative (direct address, one comma before) vs 'My brother Come here, is late' (broken apposition, needs different fix); the answer identifies WHICH comma job the sentence needs. T5: judgment call between vocative and interjection commas ('Well, Grandma, dinner is ready') where the stem quotes a sentence with THREE comma-jobs stacked and the answer picks which job the leftmost comma is doing.

framing_note: The load-bearing exemplar of the whole grammar bank. Every rung QUOTES the punchline sentence in the stem -- Comma-Saves-Lives scene-in-stem. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a kid genuinely laughs at 'Let's eat Grandma!' and never forgets the rule) and T2 ('I love cooking my family' as a horrifying admission). Vocab-teaching invariant: 'vocative' MUST be defined in the stem via the quoted example, or paired with 'comma of direct address' as inline gloss. Distractors = other real comma jobs (Oxford, appositive, non-restrictive-clause, coordinate-adjective) -- other REAL missing-comma mistakes, not joke options. Kid-safe: the Grandma gag is the ONE canonical exception to the no-fresh-violent-examples rule (it stays because it's obviously absurd, load-bearing, and Brandon's kids will not read it as violence).

name: The Oxford comma: strippers, JFK, and Stalin
scope: The serial (Oxford / Harvard) comma before the final 'and' in a list. T1: the canonical quoted contrast -- 'I invited the strippers, JFK, and Stalin' (with Oxford comma: three separate groups) vs 'I invited the strippers, JFK and Stalin' (without: JFK and Stalin ARE the strippers). Answer names the Oxford (serial) comma and its disambiguating job. T2: the apocryphal book-dedication gag -- 'To my parents, Ayn Rand and God' -- fix by adding the Oxford comma so the parents are not being named as Ayn Rand and God. T2b: the AP Stylebook (news writing) vs Chicago Manual of Style (books) split -- AP DROPS the Oxford comma by default (except where ambiguity would result), Chicago KEEPS it always; the stem quotes a wire-service headline and asks which house style it follows. T3: the O'Connor v. Oakhurst Dairy case (Maine, 2018) -- a missing Oxford comma in a state overtime-pay law led to a $5 million settlement for the drivers; the stem quotes the ambiguous clause and asks what the missing comma cost. T3b: a list where the OMITTED Oxford comma changes MEANING with everyday example -- 'For breakfast I had eggs, toast and jam and coffee' -- did toast come with jam, or was jam a separate item alongside coffee? T4: distinguish serial-comma job from super-comma (semicolon) job in a list whose items themselves contain commas -- 'I have lived in Paris, France, Rome, Italy, and Athens, Greece' -- Oxford comma cannot save this; the answer is that semicolons must replace the item-separators. T5: a stem quoting a sentence where an Oxford comma would CREATE ambiguity (rare 'appositive-swallowing' case -- 'I dedicate this to my mother, Amy Tan, and God' -- with Oxford comma, Amy Tan looks like an apposition renaming the mother); the answer identifies that no punctuation rule is universally safe and Chicago recommends recasting.
source: Grokipedia 'Serial comma' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.19 (mandatory serial comma); AP Stylebook 2020 (drops serial comma except for ambiguity); O'Connor v. Oakhurst Dairy, 851 F.3d 69 (1st Cir. 2017); Lynne Truss, 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (2003) on the Oxford comma.
framing_note: The second load-bearing punchline of the bank. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (JFK and Stalin performing as strippers) and T3 (a real $5M dairy-driver case turning on ONE missing comma). Kid-safe adaptation: 'the strippers, JFK, and Stalin' is canonical and stays; if a rung feels off, swap in 'the clowns' (keep the shape). Vocab-teaching invariant: 'serial' and 'Oxford' comma both introduced via quoted example. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the ambiguous list -- do not name the rule first. Distractors = other real list-punctuation mistakes (missing conjunction, extra comma, semicolon where comma belongs). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is a rule name, all four are real punctuation-rule names.
history_overlap: Grammar owns the serial-comma rule; the Oakhurst Dairy case is a real legal footnote, not owned by history bank.

name: The comma splice: two sentences glued with just a comma
scope: One of the most-taught errors in English composition. T1: quoted contrast -- 'It was raining, we stayed inside' -- two independent clauses joined by only a comma; answer names this as a comma splice and lists the four legit fixes (period; semicolon; comma + coordinating conjunction; subordinate one clause). Vocab-teaching in-stem: an independent clause = a group of words that could stand alone as a sentence. T2: identify which of four quoted sentences IS a comma splice vs which is a legit compound sentence -- 'The dog barked, and the cat ran' (fine: comma + and) vs 'The dog barked, the cat ran' (splice). T2b: choose the best FIX for a given comma splice -- 'She loves math, she hates spelling' -- best fix uses a semicolon because the two clauses are closely related and short. T3: distinguish comma splice from RUN-ON (fused sentence, no punctuation at all -- 'It was raining we stayed inside') from FRAGMENT (missing subject or verb -- 'Because it was raining'). Stem quotes one of each and asks which is which. T4: subtle case -- comma splice with a conjunctive adverb -- 'It was late, however we kept working' -- the presence of 'however' does NOT license the comma (needs semicolon before, comma after: 'It was late; however, we kept working'). T5: the deliberate stylistic comma splice used by writers like Cormac McCarthy or in the tricolon pattern -- 'I came, I saw, I conquered' (attributed to Caesar, 47 BC) -- and the judgment that in a rhetorical tricolon of three balanced short clauses, the comma splice is a STYLISTIC device, not an error. Answer identifies the specific rhetorical figure (tricolon / asyndeton).
source: Grokipedia 'Comma splice' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.57-6.58; Strunk & White, 'The Elements of Style' rule 5 (do not join independent clauses with a comma); Suetonius, 'Lives of the Twelve Caesars' (early 2nd cent.) for the 'veni vidi vici' attribution to Caesar.
framing_note: Register-and-fix ladder with a rhetorical twist at T5. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (three near-identical broken sentences and the kid learns to see the distinct DIFFERENT ways they're broken). Vocab-teaching invariant: 'independent clause' defined in T1 stem; 'conjunctive adverb' quoted-with-example in T4. Distractors = the other three legit fixes (period, coordinating conjunction, subordination) or the other real punctuation errors (fragment, run-on). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never say 'this is a comma splice' in the stem and then ask 'what is this?'.
history_overlap: None; Caesar quote is grammatical exemplar, not history payoff.

name: Comma before a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS)
scope: The rule for commas before 'for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so' when joining independent clauses. T1: vocab-teaching stem -- the seven coordinating conjunctions have a mnemonic 'FANBOYS' (For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So); quoted example 'The rain stopped, and we went outside' shows the comma before 'and' because two independent clauses are joined. Answer names FANBOYS. T2: comma or no comma? Quoted contrast: 'I went to the store and bought milk' (NO comma -- 'bought milk' has no subject, not an independent clause) vs 'I went to the store, and I bought milk' (comma -- second clause has its own subject 'I'). T2b: identify which quoted sentence needs a FANBOYS comma. T3: the exception for SHORT independent clauses -- Chicago says the comma may be omitted when both clauses are very short and closely related: 'I came and I saw' (Chicago 6.22 allows). Answer identifies this as a judgment call, not an error. T4: distinguish coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS) from CONJUNCTIVE ADVERBS (however, therefore, moreover, consequently) which require SEMICOLONS not just commas. Quoted contrast: 'The rain stopped, so we went out' (FANBOYS, comma is fine) vs 'The rain stopped, therefore we went out' (conjunctive adverb, needs semicolon before). T5: subordinating conjunctions (because, although, since, while, if) DO NOT take a comma before them when the dependent clause FOLLOWS the independent one: 'We went out because the rain stopped' (no comma). But DO take a comma when the dependent clause LEADS: 'Because the rain stopped, we went out'. Quoted stem tests the direction rule.
source: Grokipedia 'Coordinating conjunction' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.22, 6.25; Purdue OWL punctuation guide; Strunk & White rule 4.
framing_note: Snappy-rote paradigm ladder anchored on the FANBOYS mnemonic. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (kids find it delightful/annoying that 'however' feels like 'but' but takes different punctuation). Vocab-teaching invariant: 'coordinating conjunction', 'independent clause', 'conjunctive adverb', 'subordinating conjunction' each defined via quoted example on first appearance. Distractors = other real punctuation-with-conjunction mistakes. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: lead with the quoted sentence.

name: Appositive commas: 'my brother Mark' vs 'my brother, Mark'
scope: The comma pair that marks an APPOSITIVE -- a noun phrase renaming another noun -- and the meaning difference between restrictive (no commas) and non-restrictive (commas). T1: vocab-teaching -- 'apposition' means one noun renamed by another right next to it, as in 'my friend Alice' (no commas: RESTRICTIVE, telling you WHICH friend) vs 'my only friend, Alice' (commas: NON-RESTRICTIVE, adding info). Answer names the appositive comma pair. T2: quoted contrast -- 'My brother Mark is a doctor' (I have more than one brother; specifying WHICH one) vs 'My brother, Mark, is a doctor' (I have only one brother; his name is added info). Answer explains the meaning difference. T2b: which sentence tells you the speaker has multiple brothers? T3: proper-noun apposition where commas are almost always required -- 'The capital of France, Paris, is beautiful' -- because there is only ONE capital of France, so 'Paris' is non-restrictive. T4: professional titles -- 'The president Abraham Lincoln' (wrong for someone who has served -- there have been many presidents) vs 'President Abraham Lincoln' (title-as-name, no commas) vs 'the president, Abraham Lincoln,' (commas around the name as non-restrictive apposition). T5: nested appositives -- 'My uncle, the doctor, Frank, is here' vs 'My uncle the doctor Frank is here' -- when TWO appositions stack, the comma rules require careful nesting; the stem quotes a sentence with ambiguous nesting and the answer picks the reading that matches the punctuation.
source: Grokipedia 'Apposition' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.28 (nonrestrictive apposition); Strunk & White rule 3; Purdue OWL on restrictive vs non-restrictive.
framing_note: Vocab-heavy ladder -- apposition is a category term the bank must TEACH, not assume. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (a comma tells you how many brothers the speaker has). Every T1-T3 rung quotes the sentence and defines the term in-context. Distractors = other real comma jobs (Oxford, vocative, coordinate-adjective, non-restrictive clause). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never say 'this appositive needs commas' in the stem and then ask 'what does this appositive need?'.
history_overlap: None; Lincoln quote is grammatical exemplar.

name: Restrictive vs non-restrictive clauses (that vs which)
scope: The comma rule that distinguishes essential-to-meaning clauses (no commas, often 'that') from added-info clauses (commas, 'which' in American usage). T1: vocab-teaching -- a restrictive clause tells you WHICH one (essential, no commas); a non-restrictive clause adds extra info (set off by commas). Quoted contrast: 'The dog that bit me ran off' (restrictive: which dog?) vs 'The dog, which bit me, ran off' (non-restrictive: the dog we already know about, incidentally he bit me). T2: which sentence implies there is only ONE dog? Answer: the one with commas ('which'), because the info is added not defining. T2b: fix the punctuation -- 'The book which I read yesterday was great' -- in American formal usage, restrictive should use 'that' and no commas: 'The book that I read yesterday was great'. T3: proper-noun test -- with a UNIQUE noun (a proper name), the clause is almost always non-restrictive: 'Chicago, which sits on Lake Michigan, has cold winters' (commas required) vs (wrong) 'Chicago that sits on Lake Michigan has cold winters'. T4: British vs American usage -- British writers often use 'which' for both restrictive and non-restrictive; American style guides (Chicago, AP) prescribe 'that' for restrictive and 'which' for non-restrictive with commas. Stem quotes a British sentence and asks which house style it follows. T5: subtle cases where the SAME sentence has two valid readings depending on punctuation -- 'The students who studied passed' (restrictive: only those who studied) vs 'The students, who studied, passed' (non-restrictive: all students studied, all passed). Answer identifies both meanings.
source: Grokipedia 'English relative clauses' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.27 (commas with which); Fowler's 'Modern English Usage' on that/which; Strunk & White rule 3.
framing_note: Meaning-changing punctuation ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the SAME sentence means two different things depending on where the commas go). Vocab-teaching: 'restrictive' and 'non-restrictive' defined via quoted example. Distractors = other real clause-punctuation mistakes. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: quote the sentence first.

name: Coordinate-adjective commas: 'a small, red ball'
scope: The rule for putting commas between two adjectives modifying the same noun -- and the two tests to know when to. T1: vocab-teaching -- coordinate adjectives independently modify the same noun and can be reordered or joined by 'and'; example 'a bright, sunny day' (bright and sunny; sunny and bright -- both fine, so use a comma). Non-coordinate ('cumulative') adjectives cannot: 'a small red ball' (not 'red small ball', not 'small and red ball' comfortably -- no comma). Answer names the coordinate comma. T2: the two tests -- if you can (a) swap the order or (b) insert 'and' between them and it still sounds right, use a comma. Stem quotes 'a friendly happy dog' and asks whether it needs a comma; answer: yes (friendly and happy; happy and friendly). T2b: 'an old wooden chair' -- no comma (you would not say 'a wooden old chair' or 'an old and wooden chair'). T3: adjective-ORDER rule (English orders adjectives: opinion > size > age > shape > colour > origin > material > purpose > noun) -- 'a lovely little old rectangular green French silver whittling knife' is the canonical joke example. Answer identifies that native speakers follow this order automatically; violating it sounds broken. T4: cumulative-and-coordinate MIXED -- 'a beautiful old French painting' -- some adjectives are coordinate, some cumulative; comma placement depends on which pair passes the swap test. T5: the borderline judgment cases where either punctuation is defensible -- 'a bright yellow sun' vs 'a bright, yellow sun' -- and the style-guide advice (Chicago: use the swap test; when in doubt, no comma).
source: Grokipedia 'Adjective' and 'English grammar' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.36; Mark Forsyth, 'The Elements of Eloquence' (2013) for the adjective-order example; Purdue OWL on coordinate vs cumulative adjectives.
framing_note: Snappy paradigm ladder with a memorable T3 payoff. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the eight-adjective sequence that native speakers get right without knowing why). Vocab-teaching: 'coordinate' and 'cumulative' adjectives defined via example in T1-T2. Distractors = other real adjective-punctuation mistakes.

name: Commas in addresses: 'Springfield, Illinois'
scope: The place-and-state comma pair -- with the frequently-forgotten SECOND comma after the state. T1: quoted example -- 'She grew up in Springfield, Illinois, and moved east'. There are TWO commas: one after the city, one after the state, when the state is followed by more sentence. Answer identifies both commas as required. T2: the common error -- forgetting the second comma: 'She grew up in Springfield, Illinois and moved east' (wrong -- needs comma after 'Illinois'). Stem quotes the broken version and asks what's missing. T2b: state at END of sentence -- 'She grew up in Springfield, Illinois.' -- only ONE comma is needed; the period does the second comma's job. T3: full-address formatting -- '123 Main Street, Springfield, Illinois 62701, USA' -- commas between street/city, city/state, and state-zip/country; no comma between state and zip. T4: countries and provinces -- 'She lives in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, and works remotely' -- two commas needed after 'Canada' if the sentence continues. T5: judgment-call for a single-word city-state (Vatican City, Monaco, Singapore) or a well-known-enough city where the state is redundant: 'She lives in London' (no state needed, no comma) vs 'She lives in London, Ontario' (state needed for disambiguation).
source: Grokipedia 'Comma' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.39; AP Stylebook on address formatting; Purdue OWL on commas in addresses.
framing_note: Snappy paradigm ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (adults forget the second comma constantly -- kid learns to spot it in mailing labels). Distractors = other real address-punctuation mistakes.

name: Commas in dates: 'July 4, 1776, was Independence Day'
scope: The month-day-year comma rule plus the second comma after the year. T1: quoted example 'The Declaration was signed on July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia'. TWO commas: one between day and year, one after the year when the sentence continues. Answer names the date-comma rule. T2: end-of-sentence dates take one comma: 'The Declaration was signed on July 4, 1776.' -- period does the second comma's job. T2b: month-YEAR (no day) takes NO comma: 'in July 1776' (not 'in July, 1776'). Common error to add one; answer identifies the (missing) day as the trigger. T3: day-month-year (European / military format) takes NO commas: '4 July 1776' -- because the year already sits at the end without a preceding number that needs separating. Chicago and AP both accept both formats but prefer the American 'July 4, 1776' in running text. T4: century phrases -- 'the 1970s' (no apostrophe -- see the apostrophe ladder), 'in the 20th century', 'in mid-July 2020' -- no commas needed inside these phrases. T5: date range with dash -- 'April 12, 1861 -- April 9, 1865' (US Civil War) -- Chicago recommends an en-dash between full dates and NO extra commas inside the range. Stem quotes the full range and asks about punctuation between elements.
source: Grokipedia 'Date and time notation' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.38, 9.36; AP Stylebook 2020 on dates; Strunk & White rule 3.
framing_note: Snappy paradigm ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2b (the counterintuitive rule that 'July 1776' takes NO comma but 'July 4, 1776' does). Distractors = other real date-formatting mistakes.
history_overlap: None; the 1776 example is grammatical, not the history payoff.

name: Introductory-phrase commas: 'After dinner, we went out'
scope: The comma after an introductory word, phrase, or clause. T1: quoted example 'After dinner, we walked the dog' -- the comma marks the end of the introductory prepositional phrase and the start of the main clause. Answer names the introductory comma. T2: introductory subordinate clause (dependent clause leading the sentence) always takes a comma: 'When the rain stopped, we went out'. Contrast: 'We went out when the rain stopped' (no comma -- subordinate clause follows). Stem tests the direction rule (see also FANBOYS ladder T5). T2b: short-phrase JUDGMENT call -- Chicago allows omission when the intro is very short and cannot be misread: 'In 1776 the colonies declared independence' (comma optional). T3: introductory ADVERB commas -- 'However, we kept going' (comma required after sentence-initial 'however'); 'Meanwhile, at the ranch' (comma required); 'Yesterday I forgot' (comma optional -- one-word time adverbs are borderline). T4: interjection commas -- 'Well, that was odd', 'Oh, I see', 'Yes, please' -- all take commas after the interjection. Stem quotes a sentence without the comma and asks what's missing. T5: the AMBIGUOUS introductory-participle case where omitting the comma creates a garden-path -- 'While eating the cat watched TV' (wrong reading: while-somebody-eating-the-cat) vs 'While eating, the cat watched TV'. Answer identifies the meaning change and links to the dangling-modifier ladder.
source: Grokipedia 'Comma' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.31-6.32; Strunk & White rule 3; Purdue OWL on introductory commas.
framing_note: Ladder that pairs paradigm cases with a T5 garden-path payoff. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the missing comma turns eating-a-meal into eating-a-cat). Distractors = other real intro-punctuation mistakes. Cross-links to the dangling-modifier ladder in the P4 strand.

name: Its vs it's: the apostrophe that flips meaning
scope: The single most-misused apostrophe pair in English. T1: quoted contrast -- 'It's raining' (contraction: 'it is raining') vs 'Its raining' (wrong -- possessive 'its' + noun, does not parse as a sentence). Answer identifies 'it's' as ONLY the contraction of 'it is' (or 'it has'); 'its' as ONLY the possessive. T2: fix the errors -- 'The dog wagged it's tail' (wrong; possessive, no apostrophe: 'its'). Stem quotes the broken sentence and asks the correction. T2b: 'Its been a long day' (wrong; contraction of 'it has', needs apostrophe: 'It's'). T3: memory trick -- the possessive pronouns his, hers, its, ours, yours, theirs NEVER take apostrophes (parallel to 'his' having no apostrophe). Stem quotes 'her's / hers', 'their's / theirs' etc. and asks the pattern. T4: three-way trap with 'its', 'it's', and 'its'' -- the third form (double apostrophe) is NEVER correct in modern English; 'its' has no plural possessive because 'it' is singular. Stem quotes 'The bird flew back to its' nest' and identifies the extra apostrophe as always wrong. T5: 'it's' as contraction of 'it HAS' -- 'It's been raining all week' -- less commonly taught but grammatically valid. Stem asks which contraction the apostrophe stands for: 'is' or 'has'.
source: Grokipedia 'Apostrophe' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 7.28 (apostrophes in contractions); Lynne Truss, 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (2003) chapter on the apostrophe; Strunk & White rule 1.
framing_note: The apostrophe punchline. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (kid grasps that ONE apostrophe changes possessive to a full sentence). Vocab-teaching: 'possessive' and 'contraction' each defined via quoted example. Distractors = other real apostrophe errors (your/you're, their/they're -- see homophone strand for full ladder). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never write 'its' correctly in the stem and then ask 'what is its?'.
history_overlap: None; this rule is grammar's alone.

name: Possessive apostrophes: singular, plural, and names ending in s
scope: The possessive-apostrophe paradigm and its edge cases. T1: singular possessive adds 's -- 'the dog's bone' (one dog, one bone). Plural possessive of a regular plural adds only ' after the s -- 'the dogs' bones' (many dogs, many bones). Vocab-teaching in stem: possessive = shows ownership. T2: irregular plurals that DON'T end in s form the possessive with 's -- 'the children's toys', 'the women's room', 'the mice's tails' (not 'childrens'', 'womens'', 'mices''). Stem quotes the wrong version. T2b: fix the error -- 'The girls dresses were red' -- one girl and multiple dresses, or many girls and their dresses? Ambiguous without the apostrophe; both readings need one, in different places. T3: names ending in s -- the two accepted conventions. Chicago (2017 edition): add 's to almost all singular names ending in s: 'James's book', 'Dickens's novels', 'Jesus's disciples'. AP Stylebook: add only ' to singular proper nouns ending in s: 'James' book', 'Dickens' novels'. Stem asks which style guide is being followed. T4: joint vs separate possession -- 'John and Mary's house' (joint: they own it together, one apostrophe on the second name) vs 'John's and Mary's houses' (separate: each owns a house, apostrophe on both). Stem quotes both and asks the meaning difference. T5: the rare cases -- ancient names traditionally get only ' by convention ('Moses' law', 'Jesus' disciples', 'Achilles' heel' -- Chicago carves an exception here even in 2017); classical names ending in eez-sound also get only ' ('Xerxes' army', 'Sophocles' plays'); and inanimate possession where 'of' is preferred over 's: 'the leg of the table' (natural) over 'the table's leg' (Chicago prefers).
source: Grokipedia 'Apostrophe' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 7.16-7.20 (possessives); AP Stylebook 2020 (singular proper nouns ending in s); Strunk & White rule 1 (form the possessive singular of nouns with 's).
framing_note: Paradigm ladder with heavy style-guide split at T3-T5. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the difference between 'John and Mary's house' and 'John's and Mary's houses' matters legally). Distractors = other real apostrophe mistakes. Vocab-teaching: 'possessive', 'joint possession' defined via example. Style-guide split (Chicago vs AP) is a real editorial choice, not an error; do NOT mark rungs vision_mandated -- both are legit.

name: Apostrophes in contractions and NOT in plurals or decades
scope: The 'greengrocer's apostrophe' error and the contraction rules. T1: contractions use an apostrophe where a letter is missing -- 'don't' (do not), 'won't' (will not; irregular for 'will not' -- goes back to earlier 'woll'), 'can't' (cannot), 'shouldn't' (should not), 'we're' (we are). The apostrophe MARKS the missing letter. Answer states the rule. T2: plurals do NOT take apostrophes -- 'apples' not 'apple's', 'CDs' not 'CD's', 'the 1990s' not 'the 1990's'. The infamous 'greengrocer's apostrophe' (from British grocers writing 'apple's £1') is the canonical wrong version. Stem quotes a grocer's sign and asks what's wrong. T2b: decades take no apostrophe -- 'the 1970s', 'the '80s' (with a leading apostrophe marking the missing '19'). Stem contrasts 'the 1970s' vs 'the 1970's'. T3: TWO letters missing? Still one apostrophe -- 'shouldn't've' (should not have) has TWO apostrophes because TWO different contractions stack (n't = not, 've = have). T4: the odd contractions -- 'won't' is not 'willn't' (Old English 'wol' + not -> woll not -> won't); 'ain't' is regarded as non-standard by all major style guides but is grammatically consistent (am not / are not / is not -> ain't); 'shan't' (shall not) has TWO apostrophes' worth of missing letters (a and l) but only ONE apostrophe by convention. T5: pluralizing individual letters and abbreviations -- 'mind your p's and q's' (traditional apostrophe for single-letter plurals to avoid 'ps' looking like a word); 'the 3 R's' (apostrophe to clarify); but 'CDs' 'IDs' 'URLs' (no apostrophe; multi-letter abbreviations pluralize cleanly). Stem asks which pluralizations traditionally use apostrophes for clarity.
source: Grokipedia 'Apostrophe' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 7.28-7.29, 7.15 (plurals of letters); Lynne Truss, 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (2003) on the greengrocer's apostrophe; Strunk & White rule 1.
framing_note: Anti-error ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the greengrocer's sign 'apple's £1' feels obviously wrong and a kid learns to spot it everywhere). Vocab-teaching: 'contraction' defined via quoted example; 'greengrocer's apostrophe' introduced in-context. Distractors = other real apostrophe errors.

name: Semicolons: joining independent clauses
scope: The primary job of the semicolon -- joining two closely-related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. T1: vocab-teaching -- a semicolon joins two independent clauses (each could stand alone) when the ideas are closely related enough that a period feels too strong. Quoted example: 'It was late; we kept working' (fine; two related sentences). Answer names the semicolon's clause-joining job. T2: semicolon vs comma splice -- 'It was late, we kept working' (WRONG: comma splice, see comma-splice ladder) vs 'It was late; we kept working' (right). Stem quotes both. Fix the splice using a semicolon. T2b: identify which quoted sentence uses the semicolon CORRECTLY. T3: semicolon canNOT join an independent clause to a dependent clause -- 'It was late; because we kept working' (wrong; the second is a fragment). Rule: BOTH sides of a semicolon must be independent clauses. T4: semicolon vs COLON in joining two clauses -- semicolon = related ideas of equal weight; colon = second clause explains, expands, or is a consequence of the first. Quoted contrast: 'She has one goal; she wants to win' (semicolon, related) vs 'She has one goal: she wants to win' (colon, second explains first). Both defensible; the colon leans explanatory. T5: RHETORICAL semicolon stacking for parallelism -- 'Some go by sea; some by land; some by air' -- the semicolons enforce parallel structure across three punchy clauses. Answer identifies the rhetorical effect (parallelism, tricolon) enabled by the semicolon.
source: Grokipedia 'Semicolon' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.56; Strunk & White rule 5; Lynne Truss, 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (2003) chapter on the semicolon; Kurt Vonnegut's famous dismissal of semicolons in 'A Man Without a Country' (2005) -- note as writer-preference, not grammatical rule.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the semicolon. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (semicolon is the SIMPLE fix for the comma splice error that everybody makes). Vocab-teaching: 'independent clause' defined via example. Distractors = other real punctuation-between-clauses choices (period, comma + FANBOYS, colon).
history_overlap: None; Vonnegut opinion is writer's-preference exemplar, not literature payoff.

name: Semicolons before conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore)
scope: The rule that conjunctive adverbs need a semicolon before them (not just a comma) when joining independent clauses. T1: vocab-teaching -- conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, furthermore, meanwhile, thus, hence, indeed) are ADVERBS that connect two independent clauses. They REQUIRE a semicolon before AND a comma after: 'It was late; however, we kept working'. Answer identifies the semicolon-comma pair. T2: the comma-splice trap -- 'It was late, however we kept working' (WRONG: this is a comma splice; 'however' is not a coordinating conjunction). Fix by replacing the comma with a semicolon and adding a comma after 'however'. Stem quotes broken version. T2b: identify which of four quoted sentences punctuates the conjunctive adverb correctly. T3: sentence-initial conjunctive adverbs -- when 'However' starts a NEW sentence (period before), it takes only a comma AFTER: 'It was late. However, we kept working.' No semicolon (there is a period). Stem contrasts sentence-joining vs sentence-initial. T4: LIST of common conjunctive adverbs -- the answer distinguishes conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover) from FANBOYS coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) from SUBORDINATING conjunctions (because, although, since, while, if). Each takes different punctuation. T5: the mid-clause 'however' as a parenthetical adverb -- 'We, however, kept working' -- takes commas on both sides (not a semicolon situation; it interrupts one clause). Stem quotes each of three positions (sentence-joining, sentence-initial, mid-clause) and asks which punctuation each takes.
source: Grokipedia 'Conjunctive adverb' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.57; Purdue OWL on semicolons and conjunctive adverbs; Strunk & White rule 5.
framing_note: The trickiest single semicolon rule -- adults get this wrong constantly. Dinner-test payoff: T2 ('however' feels like a coordinating conjunction but takes different punctuation, and a semicolon is the fix). Distractors = other real punctuation-with-adverb mistakes.

name: Semicolons as super-commas in complex lists
scope: The second major job of the semicolon -- separating list items that themselves contain commas. T1: vocab-teaching -- when list items contain internal commas, ordinary comma-separation makes the list unreadable. Semicolons serve as super-commas to keep items distinct. Quoted example: 'I have lived in Paris, France; Rome, Italy; and Athens, Greece.' Answer names the super-comma job. T2: fix the broken version -- 'I have lived in Paris, France, Rome, Italy, and Athens, Greece' -- ambiguous (is 'France, Rome' one item or two?); replace item-separating commas with semicolons. T2b: identify which of four quoted lists correctly uses super-commas. T3: super-commas in a list of appositive-heavy items -- 'The speakers were Dr. Alice Chen, our chief scientist; Mr. Ben Ortiz, the operations director; and Prof. Carla Vega, the department head'. Each item has an appositive with internal commas; semicolons keep speakers distinct. T4: super-commas in DATE lists or ADDRESS lists -- 'Deadlines are July 4, 1776; December 7, 1941; and September 11, 2001'; without semicolons the date commas run into the item commas. T5: judgment call -- when the internal commas are LIGHT (single-appositive per item), some editors accept ordinary commas: 'She invited her sister, Anna, her brother, Ben, and her mother, Carla' -- ambiguous; Chicago prefers semicolons for clarity even here. Stem quotes an ambiguous list and asks the best fix.

framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the super-comma job. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the moment a kid realises the ordinary-comma version is ACTUALLY unreadable). Distractors = other real list-punctuation choices.

name: Colons: introducing lists, quotes, and explanations
scope: The three main jobs of the colon and the rule that colons should follow independent clauses. T1: vocab-teaching -- a colon introduces a list, a quote, or an explanation. Quoted example: 'She packed three things: a book, a hat, and snacks.' Answer names the colon's introducing job. T2: the RULE -- what comes BEFORE a colon must be an independent clause. Quoted contrast: 'She packed a book, a hat, and snacks' (list without colon, fine) vs 'She packed: a book, a hat, and snacks' (WRONG: 'She packed' by itself is a fragment when introducing; add 'three things' or drop the colon). Stem quotes broken version. T2b: fix the colon-after-fragment error. T3: colon introducing a quote -- 'Lincoln said: "Four score and seven years ago..."' Colon is used when the introducing sentence is a full clause; comma when it's a speaker-tag: 'Lincoln said, "Four score..."' Stem contrasts the two. T4: colon introducing an EXPLANATION or ELABORATION -- 'She had one goal: to win the race' (colon signals second clause explains first). Compare to semicolon (related but not explaining). Stem quotes both. T5: capitalisation AFTER a colon -- Chicago says lowercase after a colon unless what follows is a complete sentence AND you want to emphasise it OR it's a quote or a proper noun. AP says capitalise if what follows is a complete sentence. Stem asks which style is being followed given a quoted example.
source: Grokipedia 'Colon (punctuation)' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.61-6.64; AP Stylebook 2020 on colons; Strunk & White rule 5.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the colon. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the frequently-broken 'colon after fragment' rule that even good writers miss). Vocab-teaching: 'independent clause' reiterated via example. Distractors = other real punctuation-choices for introducing (comma, semicolon, dash).

name: Colons in time, ratios, and Bible references
scope: The technical uses of the colon outside sentence-building. T1: time -- '3:45 PM' uses a colon between hours and minutes; '3:45:30' between hours-minutes-seconds. No space around the colon. Answer names the time-colon convention. T2: ratios -- '2:1' (two to one), '3:2:1' (three-way ratio), 'sold at 5:4 odds'. No space around the colon. Stem quotes 'two to one' in prose and asks for the numeric form. T2b: fix a spaced ratio '2 : 1' (space around colon is nonstandard in American usage; some scientific journals do use spaced ratios). T3: Bible references -- 'John 3:16' (chapter 3, verse 16); 'Matthew 5:3-12' (chapter 5, verses 3 to 12); 'Genesis 1:1' (opens the Bible). No space around the colon. Answer identifies the chapter-verse colon convention. T4: Bible reference edge cases -- 'Psalm 23:1-6' (single psalm, verses 1-6), 'Psalms 23-25' (multiple psalms, no verse), 'Rev. 21:1-22:5' (spans chapters); the colon appears only when a verse number is present. Stem quotes each variant and asks which one uses the colon and why. T5: TITLE-and-SUBTITLE colons -- 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves: The Zero Tolerance Approach to Punctuation' -- colon separates main title from subtitle. Chicago capitalises the first word of the subtitle. Stem asks about capitalisation and space conventions.

name: Quotation marks: American vs British punctuation placement
scope: The transatlantic split on where periods and commas go relative to closing quotation marks. T1: vocab-teaching -- in AMERICAN usage, periods and commas ALWAYS go INSIDE closing quotation marks, even if the punctuation is not part of the quoted material: 'She said "hello."' Answer names the American rule. T2: BRITISH usage puts periods and commas OUTSIDE closing quotation marks when the punctuation is not part of the quote: 'She said "hello".' Stem contrasts American vs British. T2b: identify which quoted passage is American vs British style. T3: colons and semicolons ALWAYS go OUTSIDE the closing quotation marks in BOTH styles: 'She whispered "come here"; then she vanished'. Stem quotes the wrong (inside) version and asks the fix. T4: question marks and exclamation points depend on WHOSE question it is -- inside if the QUOTED material is a question ('She asked, "Are you coming?"'), outside if the WHOLE sentence is a question about the quoted material ('Did she say "come here"?'). Stem quotes both and asks the meaning difference. T5: American logical-punctuation adoption in TECHNICAL writing -- some American style guides (Linguistic Society of America, some tech-writing houses) use British-style logical punctuation for precision in quoting code, commands, or technical strings. Answer identifies this as a domain-specific exception, not a general rule.
source: Grokipedia 'Quotation marks in English' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.9-6.11 (American style); Fowler's 'Modern English Usage' (British style); AP Stylebook 2020; Linguistic Society of America style guide (logical punctuation).
framing_note: Paradigm ladder that teaches a transatlantic difference. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the meaning-changing question-mark placement is a genuine puzzle). Distractors = other real quote-punctuation choices.

name: Single vs double quotation marks and nested quotes
scope: The nesting convention and the transatlantic default. T1: AMERICAN usage -- DOUBLE quotes for main quotation, SINGLE quotes for a quote INSIDE a quote: 'She said, "He told me, ''hello.''"' Answer names the outer-double, inner-single American convention. T2: BRITISH usage -- historically the reverse: SINGLE quotes outer, DOUBLE inner ('She said, ''He told me, "hello."''), though modern British usage varies (Oxford now allows either as house style). Stem contrasts. T2b: identify which nesting is American vs British. T3: further nesting (rare) -- triple-nested quotes alternate: 'outer double, inner single, innermost double' in American; the reverse in British. Stem quotes a triple-nested passage. T4: SCARE quotes -- single or double quotes around a word to signal distance or irony: 'the so-called "expert"' or 'the so-called ''expert'''. Overuse is a style problem; both singles and doubles are acceptable. Chicago prefers double for scare quotes in American English. T5: SINGLE quotes for TECHNICAL / DOMAIN-SPECIFIC terms -- linguistic glossing ('the word ''cat'' has three letters'), philosophical use-mention distinction, botanical cultivar names ('Rosa ''Peace'''). These are conventions of specific domains, not general rules. Stem asks which domain a quoted convention comes from.
source: Grokipedia 'Quotation marks in English' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.11, 13.30 (single quotes for glosses); Oxford Style Manual (British convention); Fowler's 'Modern English Usage'.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for quote nesting. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (three-deep nesting is a real puzzle when it happens). Distractors = other real quote-mark conventions.

name: Block quotes and dialogue tag punctuation
scope: Long quotations and how to punctuate speaker-tags in dialogue. T1: BLOCK QUOTES -- Chicago recommends setting quotations of 100+ words (or five or more lines of poetry, or a dialogue exchange) as a BLOCK quote: indented, no surrounding quotation marks, often single-spaced or reduced-size. Answer identifies when to block-quote. T2: DIALOGUE TAG comma -- 'She said, "hello."' -- the comma before the opening quote separates the speaker-tag from the quoted speech. In American style, the closing period goes inside the quote. Answer identifies the tag-comma and the closing-period-inside rule. T2b: fix the missing tag comma -- 'She said "hello."' (wrong; needs comma after 'said'). T3: TAG POSITION -- speaker tag BEFORE the quote takes a comma before opening quote; tag AFTER the quote takes a comma before closing quote (which goes INSIDE in American style): 'She said, "hello."' vs '"Hello," she said.' Stem contrasts. T4: TAG IN MIDDLE of a quote -- 'She said, "come here," and then she vanished' -- the tag interrupts a single quoted sentence with commas around it. Contrast: '"Come here," she said. "I have news."' -- two sentences in the quote, so period ends the first, capital 'I' begins the second. Stem asks about capitalisation. T5: DIALOGUE without tags -- new paragraph indicates new speaker in prose fiction; no 'he said' needed if context is clear. Stem quotes an untagged dialogue passage and asks which speaker is saying what based on paragraph breaks.
source: Grokipedia 'Quotation marks in English' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 13.10 (block quotes), 6.40-6.42 (dialogue tags); Strunk & White rule 5.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for dialogue punctuation. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (a kid learning that paragraph breaks tell you who is speaking in a novel). Distractors = other real dialogue-punctuation choices.

name: Em-dash: the parenthetical break
scope: The em-dash and its role for strong parenthetical interruptions. T1: vocab-teaching -- an em-dash (--) is a horizontal line the width of a lowercase 'm'. It marks a sharp parenthetical break in a sentence: 'The plan -- which had taken months -- finally worked'. Answer names the em-dash and its parenthetical job. T2: em-dashes vs commas vs parentheses for parentheticals -- all three work; each has a different STRENGTH. Commas = mild interruption, parentheses = quieter aside, em-dashes = dramatic interruption. Stem contrasts three versions of the same sentence. T2b: which version is the most emphatic? T3: em-dash for a break in thought or an interrupted sentence -- 'I was going to say -- but never mind'. Answer names this dramatic-break use. T4: SPACES around em-dashes -- Chicago says NO spaces: 'plan--which took'. AP says spaces: 'plan -- which took'. Both are accepted; the choice is house style. Stem quotes both and asks which style. T5: em-dash for attribution at the end of a quote -- '"To be or not to be..." --Shakespeare' (or with space, '-- Shakespeare'). Chicago uses em-dash then attribution. Stem quotes a Shakespeare epigraph with attribution and asks the convention.
source: Grokipedia 'Dash' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.85-6.94; AP Stylebook 2020 on em-dashes; Strunk & White rule 3 (dash for parenthetical).
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the em-dash. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a kid learns that dashes are for drama -- the wound-up sentence break that ellipsis trails off). Vocab-teaching: 'em-dash' defined by width (the m-width mnemonic). Distractors = other real parenthetical-punctuation choices.
history_overlap: None; Shakespeare quote is grammatical exemplar.

name: En-dash: for ranges (pages, dates, scores)
scope: The en-dash, its width, and its four main jobs. T1: vocab-teaching -- an en-dash (-) is a horizontal line the width of a lowercase 'n' (shorter than em-dash, longer than hyphen). Primary job: RANGES. 'pp. 34-37' (pages 34 to 37); 'the years 1914-1918' (dates). Answer identifies the en-dash and its range-marking job. T2: en-dash vs hyphen -- the hyphen (-) is shorter and used for compound modifiers ('well-written'); the en-dash is used for ranges. Stem contrasts 'pp. 34-37' (correct en-dash) vs 'pp. 34-37' (hyphen -- wrong for range). Some typesetters treat these as equivalent in casual writing; Chicago distinguishes. T3: sports scores and vote counts -- '3-2 in overtime', 'the Senate voted 51-49'; en-dash by Chicago, hyphen acceptable in AP. Stem quotes a score. T4: 'Chicago -- New York flight' (en-dash for a route between two named places -- Chicago style). Also for CONNECTIONS between two equal things: 'the Bose-Einstein condensate', 'the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis'. Answer identifies this equal-connection en-dash use (note: en-dash use, not the answer content; Sapir-Whorf is a T5 distractor per grade-10 ceiling, not the payoff). T5: SPACED en-dashes as em-dash substitute -- 'the plan - which had taken months - finally worked' (British style uses spaced en-dashes where American uses unspaced em-dashes). Stem quotes both and asks the house-style difference.
source: Grokipedia 'Dash' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.78-6.84; Fowler's on British spaced-en-dash convention; AP Stylebook 2020 (does not distinguish en/em rigorously).
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the en-dash. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (three different dash-lengths for three different jobs -- a kid learns to spot which is which). Distractors = other real dash choices. Note: 'Sapir-Whorf' appears as en-dash EXAMPLE not as the answer-payoff -- linguistics jargon is not payoff (grade-10 ceiling).

name: Hyphens in compound modifiers ('well-written novel')
scope: The hyphen rule for compound modifiers before a noun, and the exceptions. T1: quoted contrast -- 'a well-written novel' (hyphen; two words together modify 'novel') vs 'the novel was well written' (no hyphen; predicate position after linking verb). Answer names the compound-modifier hyphen. T2: 'a chocolate-covered strawberry' (hyphen: compound modifier before noun) vs 'a strawberry covered in chocolate' (no compound modifier). Stem fixes the missing hyphen. T2b: 'a five-year-old boy' (two hyphens: three-word compound modifier) vs 'a boy who is five years old' (no hyphens). T3: the EXCEPTION for adverbs ending in -ly -- 'a beautifully written novel' (NO hyphen: -ly adverbs don't get hyphenated to their adjective); 'a well-written novel' (hyphen: 'well' is a one-syllable adverb, hyphenated). Stem contrasts and asks the -ly rule. T4: AMBIGUITY-BREAKING hyphens -- 'a small-business owner' (owns a small business) vs 'a small business-owner' (a small person who owns a business) vs 'a small business owner' (ambiguous). Answer identifies how the hyphen resolves the meaning. T4b: 'man-eating shark' (a shark that eats humans) vs 'man eating shark' (a man who is eating a shark) -- the missing hyphen creates a wild meaning-change punchline. T5: PREFIX hyphens -- Chicago drops hyphens after most prefixes ('preexisting', 'nonprofit', 'reelect') EXCEPT to avoid doubled vowels or ambiguity ('re-elect' when 'reelect' looks odd; 're-cover' meaning 'cover again' vs 'recover' meaning 'get well'; 'anti-inflation' to avoid 'antiinflation'). Stem quotes borderline cases and asks the Chicago rule.

name: Parentheses vs brackets: aside vs editorial insertion
scope: The distinct jobs of round parentheses () and square brackets []. T1: vocab-teaching -- parentheses (round) mark the WRITER'S own aside or clarification: 'The meeting (which lasted three hours) was productive.' Square brackets mark an EDITOR'S insertion INTO a quotation to clarify or correct: '"He [the president] arrived at noon."' Answer distinguishes the two by whose voice adds the material. T2: parentheses INSIDE parentheses -- Chicago uses square brackets for the inner nesting: '(the plan [which was long] worked)'. Some editors instead use double parens ((like this)). Stem contrasts. T3: EDITORIAL insertions in quotations -- brackets around inserted words: 'Lincoln wrote that "[the government] shall not perish"'. If a word is CHANGED (verb tense, capitalisation), brackets mark the change. Stem quotes a bracketed insertion. T4: the [sic] convention -- Latin for 'thus, so' -- placed in brackets after a QUOTED misspelling or error to signal 'this is what the original said, we didn't fix it': 'The sign read "apple's [sic] £1."' Answer identifies [sic] as an editor's note preserving an error. T5: ELLIPSIS in brackets -- '[...]' -- Chicago uses bracketed ellipsis to indicate an editor-supplied omission WITHIN a quotation, distinguishing it from an author-supplied trailing ellipsis. Stem quotes both variants and asks which is which.

name: Ellipsis: three dots vs four
scope: The dot-count rule for ellipsis in the middle vs at the end of a sentence. T1: vocab-teaching -- an ellipsis (three dots ...) marks a trailing-off in speech ('I was going to...') or an OMISSION from a quotation ('to be...that is the question'). Answer names the three-dot ellipsis and its two main jobs. T2: THREE DOTS vs FOUR -- three dots for an omission mid-sentence; FOUR dots (period + three-dot ellipsis, or three-dot ellipsis + period, depending on style) when the omission includes the end of a sentence: '"To be, or not to be: that is the question...."' (the fourth dot is the sentence-ending period). Answer explains the count-rule. T3: SPACING -- Chicago prefers spaces between the dots: '. . .'; AP uses no spaces: '...' Both are acceptable; the choice is house style. Some editors use the Unicode character (…). Stem quotes each and asks the house style. T4: BRACKETED ellipsis vs plain -- editor-supplied omission uses [...] in some styles (see brackets ladder T5); author-supplied trailing thought uses plain ...; do not confuse. Stem quotes each. T5: DIALOGUE ellipsis for trailing-off vs INTERRUPTED speech (em-dash) -- 'I was going to...' (voice trailing off, ellipsis) vs 'I was going to--' (cut off sharply by another speaker, em-dash). Answer distinguishes the two conventions and their emotional register.

name: Question marks: inside quotes, at the end, in indirect questions
scope: Placement and use of the question mark. T1: direct question ends with a question mark -- 'Where did you go?' Answer names the rule. T2: INDIRECT questions take NO question mark -- 'She asked where I went.' (statement about a question, not a question itself). Stem quotes the wrong version with a question mark and asks the fix. T2b: identify which of four sentences takes a question mark. T3: question marks INSIDE vs OUTSIDE quotation marks (see also American vs British ladder T4) -- inside when the quoted material is the question: 'She asked, "Where did you go?"'; outside when the whole sentence is a question about the quoted material: 'Did she say "come here"?' Stem contrasts. T4: TAG questions -- 'You're coming, aren't you?' -- the tag makes a statement into a question; question mark ends the whole sentence. Answer identifies the tag-question convention. T5: QUESTION WITHIN a question -- 'Did she ask, "where are you?"' -- one question mark inside for the inner question, but Chicago says NO second question mark outside; the inner mark suffices. Stem quotes both variants and asks the Chicago rule.

name: Exclamation points: use sparingly, one at a time
scope: Placement and stylistic advice for the exclamation point. T1: exclamation point ends a strong statement, command, or interjection -- 'Watch out!', 'Stop!', 'Wow!' Answer names the rule. T2: F. Scott Fitzgerald's oft-quoted advice -- 'Cut out all these exclamation points. An exclamation point is like laughing at your own joke.' Elmore Leonard's rule: 'no more than two or three per 100,000 words of prose.' Answer identifies the general style-guide preference for restraint in formal writing. T3: exclamation points INSIDE vs OUTSIDE quotation marks -- same rule as question marks: inside when the quoted material is the exclamation ('She shouted, "stop!"'); outside when the whole sentence is exclaiming about a quoted phrase ('She actually said "come here"!'). Stem contrasts. T4: MULTIPLE exclamation points -- '!!!' -- considered informal/juvenile in most style guides; Chicago and AP both recommend a single '!' for formal writing. Stem quotes the multi-mark version and asks the formal-writing rule. T5: DOUBLE PUNCTUATION -- '?!' or '!?' (the 'interrobang', combining question and exclamation) -- informal, used for incredulous questions ('You did WHAT?!'). Not standard in formal writing. Answer names the interrobang and its informal register.
