name: Panda punctuation: 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves'
scope: The canonical panda gag from Lynne Truss's 2003 book. T1: quoted contrast -- 'A panda eats shoots and leaves' (correct: a panda eats bamboo shoots and bamboo leaves, its natural diet) vs 'A panda eats, shoots, and leaves' (with commas: the panda finishes its meal, fires a gun, and departs). Answer names the comma placement as the meaning-flipper. T2: the TITLE of the book -- 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' by Lynne Truss, published in 2003 by Profile Books in the UK; a runaway bestseller that made a punctuation manual a hit book. Answer identifies the author and year. T2b: subtitle -- 'The Zero Tolerance Approach to Punctuation' -- Truss's stance was PRESCRIPTIVIST and campaigning; the book made an ethical argument for punctuation. T3: the JOKE behind the title -- Truss took the gag from an old joke about a panda entering a bar (or a cafe): the panda eats a meal, fires a gun in the air, and leaves. When asked why, the panda points at a wildlife guide that has misplaced commas after 'panda' -- 'eats, shoots and leaves' as behaviour rather than 'eats shoots and leaves' as diet. Answer explains the reader-of-the-guide framing. T4: distinguish PRESCRIPTIVISM (there IS a right answer, teach it) from DESCRIPTIVISM (record how people actually use language, don't judge) -- Truss is a proud prescriptivist; linguists (like Steven Pinker in reviews) pushed back that punctuation is historically variable. Answer names the two schools of language study. T5: OTHER commonly-cited comma-meaning-flippers Truss discusses -- 'What is this thing called love?' (a question about love) vs 'What is this thing called, love?' (asking a beloved what a thing is called); 'A woman without her man is nothing' vs 'A woman: without her, man is nothing'. Stem quotes one and asks which reading matches the punctuation.
source: Grokipedia 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (browser, 2026-09-05); Lynne Truss, 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (Profile Books UK 2003, Gotham US 2004); Steven Pinker's descriptivist reviews of the book; the original panda-bar joke (folk origin, popularised by the book).
framing_note: The load-bearing PANDA ladder -- the punchline that gave the whole prescriptivist grammar movement of the 2000s its title. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the panda literally packs a gun in the wrong-comma version) and T5 (the woman/man comma reversal). ACCURACY RAIL: Truss's book is 2003 Profile Books UK / 2004 Gotham US -- verify at build time. Vocab-teaching: 'prescriptivism' and 'descriptivism' introduced in T4 with the Truss/Pinker example. Distractors = other real punctuation-book titles and other meaning-flipping comma examples.
history_overlap: None; Truss book is a punctuation exemplar.

name: Time flies like an arrow: parsing ambiguity
scope: The classic parsing-ambiguity gag and its punctuation-based fixes. T1: quoted example -- 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana.' The first clause reads TIME [subject] FLIES [verb] LIKE AN ARROW [comparison]. The second clause looks parallel but ACTUALLY reads FRUIT FLIES [subject noun phrase: the insects] LIKE [verb: enjoy] A BANANA. Answer identifies the parsing pivot. T2: the attribution -- often attributed to Groucho Marx (though its exact origin is disputed; the gag circulates in linguistics circles from the 1960s onward, sometimes credited to Anthony Oettinger). Answer names the disputed attribution. T3: the PUNCTUATION lesson -- a well-placed hyphen COULD disambiguate the second clause ('fruit-flies' as compound noun); a comma or dash before the parallel-breaking clause can signal the pivot. Stem asks which punctuation would flag the ambiguity for a reader. T4: OTHER classic parsing-ambiguity sentences -- 'They are cooking apples' (cooking as verb: they are cooking some apples; OR cooking as adjective: they are the type of apples used for cooking). No punctuation fix; context does the work. Stem quotes and asks the two readings. T5: FRUIT FLIES vs FRUIT-FLIES -- Chicago hyphenates compound nouns only where ambiguity requires; 'fruit fly' is unhyphenated as an open compound in most dictionaries. Answer identifies the compound-noun convention and how hyphens sometimes disambiguate parsing.
source: Grokipedia 'Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana' (browser, 2026-09-05); Anthony Oettinger, 'The Uses of Computers in Science' (Scientific American, 1966) for a natural-language-processing citation; Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 7.85 on compound nouns.
framing_note: Parsing-ambiguity ladder anchored on a canonical gag. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (kid sees the pivot for the first time and thinks it's magic). ACCURACY RAIL: attribution to Groucho Marx is folk; Oettinger 1966 is a documented early linguistic citation. Distractors = other real parsing-ambiguity examples and other real compound-noun conventions.

name: Slashes: and/or, dates, and line breaks in poetry
scope: The forward slash and its main uses. T1: 'and/or' -- the slash indicates alternatives or both: 'the parent and/or guardian'. Chicago dislikes 'and/or' (recommends recasting: 'the parent, the guardian, or both'); AP accepts it in informal use. Answer names the alternative-slash convention. T2: DATES in slash notation -- '7/4/1776' (US: month/day/year) vs '4/7/1776' (UK: day/month/year) vs '1776-07-04' (ISO 8601 international standard). The AMBIGUITY of slash-dates across regions is a real communication hazard. Answer identifies the US vs UK vs ISO conventions. T3: FRACTIONS in text -- '1/2', '3/4', '1/3' -- slash for typed fractions; typeset fractions use Unicode (½, ¾). Chicago recommends spelling out fractions in prose ('one-half') and using slashes only in technical writing. T4: LINE BREAKS in poetry when QUOTED in prose -- 'Whose woods these are I think I know / His house is in the village though' -- slash marks the poem's line-break in a prose citation. Space before AND after the slash. Stem quotes a poem citation and asks the convention. T5: URL and PATH slashes -- 'https://example.com/page' (URL uses forward slashes); 'C:\Users\brand' (Windows path uses backslashes). These are technical conventions, not grammatical rules; Chicago accepts them as-is in code and citations. Answer distinguishes URL forward-slash from Windows-path backslash.
source: Grokipedia 'Slash (punctuation)' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.107-6.111 (slashes); ISO 8601 date standard; MLA Handbook on quoting poetry with slashes.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the slash. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the same date '7/4' means completely different days in the US vs UK -- travel confusion). Distractors = other real punctuation choices for alternatives, dates, and fractions.
history_overlap: None; 1776 date is a numeric exemplar.

name: Capitalization at sentence start and after colons
scope: The capitalization rules that intersect with punctuation. T1: capitalize the first word of every sentence, including sentences inside quoted dialogue: 'She said, "Come here."' Answer names the sentence-start rule. T2: capitalization AFTER a colon -- Chicago says lowercase unless what follows is a complete sentence AND you want to emphasise it OR it's a quote or proper noun. AP says capitalise if what follows is a full sentence. Stem contrasts. T2b: which style is being followed given a quoted colon-example? T3: capitalization in HEADLINES and TITLES -- title case ('The Quick Brown Fox') vs sentence case ('The quick brown fox'). Chicago capitalizes the first, last, and 'important' words in titles; AP uses similar rules for headlines. Stem quotes both and asks the convention. T4: capitalization of TITLES OF PEOPLE -- 'President Lincoln' (before name, capitalized) vs 'Lincoln, the president' (after name, lowercase); 'the president signed the bill' (generic, lowercase). Chicago and AP agree on the before/after-name split. T5: capitalization of RELATIVES -- 'my mother said' (lowercase, generic) vs 'Mother said' (capitalized, used as a proper name substitute); 'Aunt Sally' (before name, capitalized) vs 'my aunt Sally' (lowercase, 'aunt' as descriptor). Stem contrasts.
source: Grokipedia 'Capitalization' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.63 (capitalization after colon), 8.156 (titles of people), 8.158 (kinship names); AP Stylebook 2020.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for capitalization intersections. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (kid learns why 'President Lincoln' capitalizes but 'the president Abraham Lincoln' doesn't). Distractors = other real capitalization conventions. Vocab-teaching: 'title case', 'sentence case', 'proper name' each defined via example. Kid-safe: 'President Lincoln' is neutral historical, per apolitical-examples rule.

name: Italics vs quotation marks for titles
scope: Which titles get italics, which get quotation marks, and why. T1: BIG works get italics -- book titles, film titles, album titles, newspaper names, magazine names, plays, operas, TV series, ships, works of art. Example: 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (in prose, italicized as *Eats, Shoots and Leaves*); 'The New York Times' italicized. Answer names the italics-for-major-works rule. T2: SMALL works get quotation marks -- article titles, chapter titles, poem titles (short), song titles, TV episode titles. Example: 'a chapter titled "The Vocative Comma" in Truss's book'. Stem quotes both and asks which convention. T2b: which style does a short poem take? T3: EPISODE within series -- the series in italics, the episode in quotes: 'the episode "The One with the Prom Video" of Friends'. Stem asks the pairing convention. T4: FOREIGN WORDS -- italicize foreign words not yet naturalized in English: 'the phrase mise en scene'. Chicago italicizes on first use, then Roman on subsequent uses; AP italicizes only if unfamiliar. Stem contrasts. T5: SHIPS, TRAINS, and SPACECRAFT -- italicized: 'the Titanic', 'the Orient Express', 'the Apollo 11 command module Columbia'. But the CLASS name (a type of ship, not an individual) is not italicized: 'a Ford-class carrier' vs 'the USS Gerald R. Ford'. Stem asks the individual-vs-class distinction.
source: Grokipedia 'Italic type' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 8.156-8.201 (titles of works); MLA Handbook 9th ed. on titles; AP Stylebook 2020.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the italics/quotes split. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (episode-within-series pairing). Distractors = other real title-formatting conventions.

name: Punctuation with abbreviations: US vs U.S. vs USA
scope: The period-in-abbreviations rules and their style-guide splits. T1: TITLES before names -- Dr. Smith, Mr. Ortiz, Ms. Chen, Mrs. Vega -- take periods in AMERICAN usage. Chicago 17th ed. accepts both 'Dr' (British) and 'Dr.' (American); AP uses 'Dr.' Answer names the American periods-in-titles convention. T2: DEGREES after names -- Ph.D., M.D., B.A., M.A. -- Chicago now recommends NO periods ('PhD', 'MD', 'BA') as of the 17th edition; older Chicago and most other style guides retain periods. Stem contrasts. T2b: which of four quoted degree abbreviations follows the modern Chicago convention? T3: COUNTRY abbreviations -- U.S. vs US, U.K. vs UK. Chicago 17th ed. drops periods ('US', 'UK'); AP retains them ('U.S.') as noun and adjective. AP note: 'US' unpunctuated is fine in headlines. Stem asks which style is being followed. T4: LATIN abbreviations -- e.g. (exempli gratia, 'for example'), i.e. (id est, 'that is'), etc. (et cetera, 'and so forth'). All take periods. Followed by comma in American usage ('e.g., a cat, a dog'), no comma in British. Stem contrasts. T5: ABBREVIATIONS at end of sentence -- 'The bill was passed by the U.S.' (period after 'S' is the abbreviation period AND the sentence-ending period -- one period does both jobs, not two). Answer names the collapsed-period rule.
source: Grokipedia 'Abbreviation' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 10.4-10.10, 10.32 (US, UK), 10.42 (degrees), 6.51 (Latin abbreviations); AP Stylebook 2020.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for abbreviation punctuation. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (one period does two jobs at end-of-sentence -- adults often add a second and are wrong). Vocab-teaching: 'abbreviation' defined via quoted example. Distractors = other real abbreviation conventions.

name: Numbers: when to spell out, when to use digits
scope: The spelled-out vs digits rules, which intersect with commas and hyphens. T1: CHICAGO general rule -- spell out numbers zero through one hundred, and round numbers ('two hundred', 'five thousand'); use digits for everything else. AP style spells out zero through nine and uses digits for 10 and up. Answer identifies the two main house styles. T2: NUMBERS starting a sentence -- always spell out, regardless of style: 'Fifteen students attended' (not '15 students attended'). Recast if the number is awkward to spell. T2b: fix a sentence starting with a digit. T3: COMMAS in large numbers -- English uses commas every three digits from the right for thousands ('1,000,000'); European convention uses periods or spaces ('1.000.000' or '1 000 000'). Chicago recommends commas in American usage. Stem contrasts. T4: HYPHENATED spelled-out numbers -- twenty-one through ninety-nine take hyphens ('forty-two', 'ninety-nine'); larger compound numbers do not ('one hundred forty-two', not 'one-hundred-forty-two'). Answer names the hyphen rule for two-digit numbers. T5: ORDINALS -- '1st', '2nd', '3rd' vs 'first', 'second', 'third'. Chicago prefers spelled-out ordinals in text ('the third floor'); AP allows digits in dates ('June 3rd' is nonstandard; both prefer 'June 3'). Superscript ordinals ('3rd') are considered informal in most style guides. Stem quotes and asks the formal convention.
source: Grokipedia 'Numeral (linguistics)' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 9.2-9.7 (spelled-out numbers), 9.55 (large-number commas), 9.6 (hyphenated compound numbers); AP Stylebook 2020 on numerals.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for number formatting. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (European vs American thousand-separator -- '1.000.000' looks like one point zero million to an American). Distractors = other real number-formatting conventions.

name: The rare punctuation marks: interrobang, pilcrow, guillemets
scope: Uncommon but real punctuation marks the kid will encounter. T1: INTERROBANG (?) -- combines question mark and exclamation point for incredulous questions: 'You did WHAT(?)' Invented by advertiser Martin K. Speckter in 1962. Not standard in formal writing; the two-character combo '?!' or '!?' is the informal equivalent. Answer names the interrobang. T2: PILCROW (para) -- the paragraph symbol, used in legal and religious texts to mark paragraph divisions when they run together in the source. Also called the paragraph mark. Answer names the pilcrow. T2b: identify the pilcrow among distractors (section symbol section, dagger dag, at-sign @, ampersand and). T3: SECTION SYMBOL (section) -- used in legal citations to reference sections of a statute: '18 U.S.C. section 1001'. Doubled 'section-section' means multiple sections: 'sections 100-105'. Answer names the section symbol. T4: GUILLEMETS (<< >>) -- angle brackets used as quotation marks in French, Spanish, Russian, and other European languages: '<<Bonjour>>, dit-il'. English uses only in scholarly citation of foreign material. Answer names the French quote conventions. T5: DAGGER (dag) and DOUBLE DAGGER (double-dag) -- footnote reference marks after asterisk (*) in the traditional Chicago footnote sequence: * dag double-dag section para hash. Modern style prefers superscript numbers, but the traditional sequence is still used in legal writing and some academic disciplines. Answer names the footnote-mark sequence.
source: Grokipedia 'Interrobang', 'Pilcrow', 'Section sign', 'Guillemet', 'Dagger (mark)' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 14.24 (footnote reference marks), 11.3 (guillemets in foreign languages); Martin K. Speckter's 1962 TYPEtalks Magazine article proposing the interrobang.
framing_note: T5-heavy ladder on rare marks -- earned only after the common-mark ladders. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a whole punctuation mark invented by an advertising executive in 1962). Vocab-teaching: each mark named and shown via quoted example. Distractors = other real rare punctuation marks.

name: Punctuation with parenthetical asides: commas, dashes, or parens
scope: Choosing among the three punctuation options for a parenthetical interruption -- commas, em-dashes, or parentheses -- and what each choice signals. T1: three levels of interruption strength -- commas (mild, integrated), em-dashes (dramatic, emphatic), parentheses (quiet aside, backgrounded). Same sentence three ways: 'The plan, which had taken months, worked' vs 'The plan -- which had taken months -- worked' vs 'The plan (which had taken months) worked'. Answer names the three strengths. T2: identify which version is the most EMPHATIC. Which is the quietest? Which is the most neutral? T2b: rewrite an all-comma sentence to emphasize the aside; rewrite an all-dash sentence to downplay it. T3: PARENTHESES with END punctuation -- when the parenthetical is a COMPLETE sentence on its own, punctuation goes INSIDE the parens: '(She was tired.)' When the parens interrupt another sentence, punctuation goes OUTSIDE: 'She was tired (as usual).' Stem contrasts. T4: NESTED parentheticals -- avoid parens-inside-parens; use brackets for the inner: '(the plan [which was long] worked)' or recast to remove the nesting. Stem quotes an over-nested sentence and asks the fix. T5: PARENTHETICAL commas within an already-comma-heavy sentence -- shift to dashes for clarity: 'Alice, our director, who also, on occasion, sings, will speak' -> 'Alice -- our director, who also on occasion sings -- will speak'. Stem quotes the comma-cluttered version and asks the best fix.
source: Grokipedia 'Parenthesis' and 'Dash' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.95-6.106 (parentheses), 6.85-6.94 (dashes); Strunk & White rule 7.
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for the three-way parenthetical choice. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (same sentence three ways with distinctly different rhetorical effect -- a real writer's toolkit). Distractors = other real punctuation choices.

name: End punctuation with parenthetical citations
scope: The comma-and-period placement rules for in-text citations (MLA, APA, Chicago author-date). T1: MLA style -- author and page in parentheses, period AFTER the closing paren: 'The comma changes everything (Truss 12).' Answer names the MLA convention. T2: APA style -- author and year in parentheses, period AFTER: 'The comma changes everything (Truss, 2003).' Note the comma before the year in APA (not in MLA). Stem contrasts MLA vs APA. T2b: identify which citation style a quoted example follows. T3: CHICAGO author-date -- similar to APA: '(Truss 2003, 12)'; no comma between author and year in Chicago author-date. Stem contrasts. T4: CITATION at end of a QUOTED sentence -- the closing quote comes first, then the citation, then the period: 'She wrote that punctuation "changes everything" (Truss 12).' Note: the period from the original quote is DROPPED because the sentence continues past the quote to the citation. T5: LONG QUOTATIONS (block quotes) -- citation goes AFTER the closing period of the block, not inside the block. Contrast with in-line quotes where the citation goes before the sentence-ending period. Stem contrasts the two conventions.
source: Grokipedia 'Parenthetical referencing' (browser, 2026-09-05); MLA Handbook 9th ed. (2021); APA Publication Manual 7th ed. (2020); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 15.20-15.30 (author-date citations).
framing_note: Paradigm ladder for citation punctuation. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the counterintuitive rule that the original period gets DROPPED for the citation-ending period). Distractors = other real citation-style conventions. Note: this borders the writing-composition lane; keep the payoff on PUNCTUATION not on 'how to cite'.

name: Punctuation and emojis: the modern informal register
scope: Informal-register punctuation conventions that have arisen in texting and messaging. T1: the DROPPED period in single-message texts -- 'im on my way' vs 'I'm on my way.' -- in casual texting, ending a message with a period reads as CURT or ANGRY (per linguistic research on iMessage register, Gretchen McCulloch 'Because Internet' 2019). Answer identifies the register shift and notes this is INFORMAL only. T2: the ELLIPSIS in texting -- 'ok...' -- reads as PASSIVE-AGGRESSIVE or HESITANT rather than trailing-off (per McCulloch). Contrast with the formal ellipsis for omissions. Stem contrasts formal vs informal readings. T3: the ALL-CAPS convention -- shouting in text; SOME people also use ALL CAPS for emphasis of a single word within otherwise-lowercase text. Chicago and AP both regard all-caps as SHOUTING in prose; use italics for emphasis in formal writing. T4: EMOJIS after punctuation -- in modern chat, an emoji often ends a message in place of a period. If both are present, emoji goes after the period. Style guides (Chicago 17th ed. explicitly punts) don't yet have a formal rule; treat as informal register. T5: MULTIPLE PUNCTUATION for emphasis in text -- '!!!', '???', 'ok?????' -- reads as strong emotion in text; nonstandard in formal writing. Note the parallel between text-punctuation-emphasis and the interrobang for incredulous questions. Answer distinguishes the two registers.
source: Grokipedia 'Internet linguistics' (browser, 2026-09-05); Gretchen McCulloch, 'Because Internet: Understanding the New Rules of Language' (Riverhead, 2019); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.129 (informal styles); studies of iMessage / SMS register.
framing_note: Register-shift ladder on modern informal conventions. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a period at the end of 'ok.' feels angry to a teenager and neutral to a boomer -- the register split is real). Vocab-teaching: 'register' defined in-context. Distractors = other real informal-punctuation conventions. Kid-safe: no political examples; use pet/homework/weather everyday scenes.

name: Two spaces after a period? The zombie typewriter rule
scope: The one-space vs two-space debate and its typewriter origins. T1: the RULE -- modern typography uses ONE space after a period, not two. Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. (2017) explicitly requires one space. Answer identifies the modern one-space standard. T2: the HISTORY -- monospaced typewriter fonts made a single space look tight after a period, so typing teachers taught TWO spaces from the 1890s through the mid-20th century. Proportional fonts (used by all modern computers) space periods correctly with one space. Answer names the typewriter origin. T2b: which era of writers was taught two spaces? T3: the ZOMBIE-RULE frame -- 'two spaces after a period' is still enforced by some older editors and school curricula, even though every major style guide has explicitly abandoned it. Compare to other zombie rules: never split infinitives, never end with a preposition, never begin with a conjunction. Answer notes the zombie-rule pattern (rule that persists past its rationale). T4: the RESEARCH -- Skidmore College 2018 study by Rebecca Johnson et al. found that reading speed was very slightly faster with two spaces after a period for monospaced fonts, no significant difference for proportional fonts (which nearly everyone uses). Answer identifies the research finding: no benefit to two-space in modern typography. T5: HTML COLLAPSE -- HTML and web browsers collapse multiple spaces into ONE unless ' ' or CSS is used; even if you type two, the browser shows one. This finalized the death of the two-space convention for anyone writing online. Answer names the technical collapse.
source: Grokipedia 'Sentence spacing' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 2.9 (one space after a period); Johnson, Bui, Schmitt, and Franchescina, 'Are two spaces better than one?' Attention, Perception, and Psychophysics 80 (2018); AP Stylebook 2020.
framing_note: Zombie-rule debunking ladder. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the rule has a REASON -- typewriter fonts -- that vanished decades ago). Vocab-teaching: 'zombie rule', 'monospaced' vs 'proportional font' defined in-context. Distractors = other real zombie-rules (never split infinitive etc.) which are covered in their own P5 usage-and-register ladder.

name: The Grandma comma and other missing-comma horrors
scope: A curated ladder of the funniest missing-comma real-world horror examples. T1: the canonical Grandma vocative -- 'Let's eat, Grandma!' vs 'Let's eat Grandma!' -- kicks off the ladder (a shorter reprise of the P1 vocative ladder T1). T2: 'I like cooking my family and my pets.' Fix: 'I like cooking, my family, and my pets.' (Or better: recast entirely; comma won't fully save it.) Stem quotes the wrong version and asks the fix. T2b: 'Rachael Ray finds inspiration in cooking her family and her dog.' -- a real 2011 Tails Magazine cover, widely mocked online, that a comma would have fixed. T3: 'Woman: without her, man is nothing.' vs 'Woman, without her man, is nothing.' -- the classic comma-changes-meaning gag. Stem quotes both and asks the meaning difference. T3b: 'A woman without her man is nothing' (no commas) -- ambiguous; answer identifies that punctuation is what disambiguates. T4: 'The panda eats shoots and leaves' (from the P1 panda ladder T1, kept as canonical) as a summary of the whole strand. T5: judgment call -- which comma fixes actually help and which are pedantic overcorrections? Chicago says: use punctuation for CLARITY, not for ritual. Stem quotes a light-comma vs heavy-comma sentence pair and asks which is clearer.
source: Grokipedia 'Comma' (browser, 2026-09-05); Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. 6.16 (commas for clarity); Lynne Truss, 'Eats, Shoots and Leaves' (2003); the Rachael Ray Tails Magazine 2011 cover (widely reproduced online).
framing_note: The 'greatest hits' ladder for the whole punctuation strand -- reprises Grandma, panda, woman/man in a single arc for cross-reinforcement. Dinner-test payoff: EVERY rung. Kid-safe: the Grandma gag stays; Rachael Ray cooking family gag stays (obviously absurd, real published error). No fresh violent examples. Distractors = other real missing-comma horrors from the canon.
